title: Who am I (Exodus 3:11–4:17)
hook: Moses gives five excuses, including I'm slow of speech

segments.voice: Yesterday, seneh, the bush that burned and wasn't consumed, and a voice saying take off your shoes. Your line was holy ground. Where did you stand still today? Day three hundred seventy.

A toast nobody else will give. A project with one name on it. The hard conversation with a father. Some jobs arrive too big for the person asked, and the reasons it should be someone else line up fast, every one of them reasonable. Moses is standing barefoot in front of a burning bush, and God has just told him the plan: I've seen my people's misery in Egypt, I've heard their cry, and I'm sending you to Pharaoh to bring them out. And Moses, who will lead a whole people out of slavery, does what people do. He starts making excuses. Five of them.
screen: `A JOB TOO BIG.` → `I'M SENDING YOU TO PHARAOH.` → `FIVE EXCUSES.`

segments.voice: Excuse one: who am I, to go to Pharaoh? A fair question from a shepherd with a past. And God doesn't answer it. God doesn't say, you're actually very talented. God says, "I will be with thee." The answer to who am I is who goes with you. Excuse two: what if they ask your name? God gives the name, I am who am, which this path opened back in year one. Excuse three: they won't believe me. So God gives signs: the staff that becomes a snake, the hand that turns white and heals, water from the Nile that turns to blood. Excuse four is the most human: I'm not a speaker. I never have been, not before and not since you started talking to me; I'm slow of speech and slow of tongue. Some Jewish tradition and some later readers have wondered whether Moses had a stammer; the text doesn't say. God's reply is almost funny: who made a person's mouth? Go, and I'll be with your mouth. And then excuse five, with nothing left: please, Lord, send someone else. That's the one that makes God angry. And still God doesn't fire him. God sends his brother Aaron along to help him speak. Catholics hear an echo of this scene in a small house in Nazareth. An angel greets a young woman with the words, "the Lord is with thee," and gives her an impossible mission. She asks one honest question, how shall this be done, gets her answer, and says yes. Moses took five tries. The promise was the same both times: you won't go alone.
screen: `WHO AM I? I WILL BE WITH THEE.` · `THEY WON'T BELIEVE ME: SIGNS.` · `I'M SLOW OF SPEECH: WHO MADE YOUR MOUTH?` · `SEND SOMEONE ELSE: AARON GOES TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your excuse, then go anyway. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been avoiding because it feels too big: a call, an apology, a class, a conversation. Now listen to the reason you give yourself. Say it plainly, the way Moses did. I'm not good with words. I'm not the right person. They won't listen. Don't argue with it. Just name it. Then picture yourself doing the thing anyway, excuse and all, with someone beside you. If you pray, you can hear God's answer to Moses: I will be with thee. If you don't, picture a friend at your shoulder. The bell holds the time.
Who am I. Moses's first excuse at the burning bush, answered not with praise but with a promise of presence. Today's word.
Your line: I will be with thee. Today, take one small step toward the thing you've been excusing yourself from. Day three hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the angel's greeting to Mary, "the Lord is with thee," in every Hail Mary, and the Church often reads call stories like Moses's on vocation Sundays, when parishes pray for priests, religious and lay ministers.

match.prompt: match each excuse to God's answer.
pairs: the staff, the hand, the water

myth: God answers who am I by telling Moses how gifted he is
God answers with presence: I will be with thee.
the text says plainly that Moses had a stammer

fork.setup: you're Moses. you've run out of reasons. God has answered every one. what's your last line?
options: let me think about it for a year.
fork.reveal: he asks God to send someone else. God is angry, and sends him anyway, with his brother Aaron to help him speak.

original.note: Hebrew: who am I? Moses's first words of reply in Exodus 3:11.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses was a born leader.
what it means: he gave five excuses, and every answer God gave came back to one thing: I will be with thee.
what a scholar hears: object, reassure, sign: some readers trace the same call-story pattern in Gideon, Jeremiah, and Luke's annunciation.

notes: Day 295 taught 'I am who am' (Exodus 3:14); this day mentions it briefly and points back to year one rather than reteaching it.
Five excuses: 3:11, 3:13, 4:1, 4:10, 4:13. Signs: 4:2–9. Paraphrases of 4:10–12 and 4:13–16; confirm against the Douay-Rheims.

'Jewish tradition and many readers since have wondered whether Moses had a stammer': there are rabbinic/midrashic traditions (e.g., the coal story in Exodus Rabbah) about Moses's speech. Confirm phrasing.
Call-narrative pattern (Gideon, Judges 6; Jeremiah 1; Luke 1) is a standard scholarly observation; confirm the trapdoor phrasing.
Luke 1:34 'how shall this be done' used as a short phrase, unquoted.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what their mind does; unsourced superlative 'the greatest prophet of Israel' cut; 'many readers' on the stammer softened to 'some'; trapdoor call-pattern framed as some readers' observation.
